term.name: Running key cipher
term.short: A running key cipher uses a long, nonrepeating text or sequence as the keystream for polyalphabetic substitution.
term.meta_title: Running Key Cipher — Definition and Weaknesses | CiphersOnline
term.meta_description: Learn how a long text supplies a Vigenère-like keystream, how running key differs from autokey, and why natural-language keys remain vulnerable.

body.title: Definition
body.html: A running key cipher combines plaintext with a key sequence that is normally at least as long as the message. In a common form, letters from a book passage select successive Vigenère shifts instead of repeating a short keyword.

body.title: Running key and autokey
body.html: A running key comes from an external long source. Autokey starts with a short secret primer and extends it with plaintext or ciphertext. If a public book is used, the edition, passage, and starting position must effectively remain secret.

body.title: Security limits
body.html: Natural-language key text is not random: it has letter frequencies and correlations that combine with those of the plaintext. Specialized statistical attacks can exploit this structure, so the method does not provide modern security.

faq.question: Is a running key a one-time pad?
faq.answer: No. A one-time pad requires uniformly random, secret, nonreused key material; ordinary book text does not meet that requirement.

faq.question: Can the key text be reused?
faq.answer: Reuse creates additional relationships between messages and makes cryptanalysis easier.
